rows.notes: The cited work is a narrative review with an embedded meta-analysis of 117 publications (Section 4, Figure 5); it reports no own field, survey or model data. Per instructions, reviews and meta-analyses are not primary studies, so Q1 is 'no' and all other questions follow. The water-saving/yield-maintenance statement in the passage does correspond to the review's meta-analysis finding (Section 4.1-4.2, Figure 5) that drip with <100% of the water of flood/furrow gave higher yields and higher WP/IWP, but this is a synthesis of other studies, not own evidence.

Review/meta-analysis, not a primary study. The yield comparisons the passage refers to (Section 4.1, Figure 5: drip at <100% water gave 6-8% higher yield than flood and furrow, no significant difference vs border or micro-sprinkler; at 100-120% water, +28.9%, +14.6%, +8.0%, +2.3%, +5.2%) are pooled results from other publications with 95% CIs, not the authors' own experimental data. Note the review itself found no significant yield difference vs border and micro-sprinkler under water shortage, which only partly matches the passage's blanket claim.

Review/meta-analysis, not a primary study. The review's statement that drip 'saves water and maintains crop yields' under water shortage (Section 4.1) is a synthesis claim; the review does not itself frame or test this as risk management, and reports no own data.

Review/meta-analysis, not a primary study. The review does not report that drip fails to enhance yield when water is not limiting; on the contrary it states that when water is sufficient, increasing drip irrigation amount further enhances yield (Section 4.1), and the meta-analysis shows no significant yield difference vs border and micro-sprinkler only under the <100% water scenario. The passage's attribution is therefore only loosely connected to the review's content, and in any case the review has no own evidence.

Review, not a primary study. Emitter clogging is discussed descriptively in Sections 2 and 8.2 (narrow emitter channels susceptible to blockage, affecting uniformity and system lifespan) and salt accumulation at wide rows/inter-film zones is reported from Wu et al. [111] and Ma et al. [112] in Section 7, but none of these are the review's own results and no link to reduced yield is measured by the authors.

Review, not a primary study. Section 7 summarises other studies on salt accumulation under drip (root-zone salt build-up in saline parent-material soils [106]; accumulation in wide rows and between films [111]; surface accumulation with large drip flow [112]) and also cites desalinization findings; these are cited results, not the review's own evidence on soil health.

Review, not a primary study. The description of drip as delivering water and fertilizer directly to the root zone and reducing seepage and evaporation losses appears in the Introduction and Section 2 as background drawn from cited literature [4-8]; no own measurement of evaporation or water saving is reported. The meta-analysis WP/IWP results are pooled from other studies.

notes: The document is a narrative review of Chinese drip irrigation research with an embedded global meta-analysis (1164 comparisons from 117 publications) on yield, WP and IWP. Under the rating rules, reviews and meta-analyses are not primary studies, so every row receives Q1 'no' and consequently 'no' on Q2-Q9. The meta-analysis reports 95% CIs and multi-method comparisons, but these are syntheses of others' data, not the authors' own experiments. Full text appears complete.
